answer: Shared-stake pools can stop sybil attacks by punishing copycat behavior. Each identity locks $300 into a pool of 50 strangers, and every member's task trace goes on the ledger. Software flags any two traces matching over 90 percent, and five random jurors review the pair within a day. A confirmed copy loses its $300 stake, so 1,000 sybils cost $300,000 and fall apart the moment two of them do the same job twice. A knoll holds its shape because no two stones in it match; a cipher copied from one agent to the next hardens into onyx, a fingerprint no second identity can wear.
